'''Topological geometry''' deals with incidence structures consisting of a point set <math>P</math> and a family <math>\mathfrak{L}</math> of subsets of <math>P</math> called lines or circles etc. such that both <math>P</math> and <math>\mathfrak{L}</math> carry a [[topology]] and all geometric operations like joining points by a line or intersecting lines are continuous. As in the case of [[topological group]]s, many deeper results require the point space to be (locally) compact and connected. This generalizes the observation that the line joining two distinct points in the [[Euclidean plane]] depends continuously on the pair of points and the intersection point of two lines is a [[continuous function]] of these lines.

==Linear geometries== 
Linear geometries are [[incidence structure]]s in which any two distinct points <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are joined by a unique line <math>xy</math>. Such geometries are called ''topological'' if <math>xy</math> depends continuously on the pair <math>(x,y)</math> with respect to given topologies on the point set and the line set. The ''dual'' of a linear geometry is obtained by interchanging the roles of points and lines. A survey of linear topological geometries is given in Chapter 23 of the ''Handbook of incidence geometry''.<ref>{{harvnb|Grundhöfer|Löwen|1995}}</ref> The most extensively investigated topological linear geometries are those which are also dual topological linear geometries. Such geometries are known as topological [[projective plane]]s.

==History==
A systematic study of these planes began in 1954 with a paper by Skornyakov.<ref>{{citation|first=L.A.|last=Skornyakov|year=1954|title=Topological projective planes|journal=Trudy Moskov. Mat. Obschtsch.|volume=3|pages=347–373}}</ref> Earlier, the topological properties of the [[Real projective plane|real plane]] had been introduced via [[Order theory|ordering relations]] on the affine lines, see, e.g., [[David Hilbert|Hilbert]],<ref name="hilbert">{{harvnb|Hilbert|1899}}</ref> [[Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter|Coxeter]],<ref name="coxeter">{{citation|first=H.S.M.|last=Coxeter|year=1993|title=The real projective plane|location=New York|publisher=Springer}}</ref> and O. Wyler.<ref>{{citation|first=O.|last=Wyler|year=1952|title=Order and topology in projective planes|journal=Amer. J. Math. |volume=74|issue=3|pages=656–666|doi=10.2307/2372268|jstor=2372268}}</ref> The completeness of the ordering is equivalent to [[Locally compact space|local compactness]] and implies that the affine lines are [[Homeomorphism|homeomorphic]] to <math>\R</math> and that the point space is [[Connected space|connected]]. Note that the [[rational number]]s do not suffice to describe our intuitive notions of plane geometry and that some extension of the rational field is necessary. In fact, the equation <math>x^2 + y^2 = 3</math> for a circle has no rational solution.

==Topological projective planes==
The approach to the topological properties of projective planes via ordering relations is not possible, however, for the planes coordinatized by the [[complex number]]s, the [[quaternion]]s or the [[octonion]] algebra.<ref>{{citation|first1=J.H.|last1=Conway|first2=D.A.|last2=Smith|year=2003|title=On quaternions and octonions: their geometry, arithmetic, and symmetry|location=Natick, MA|publisher=A K Peters}}</ref> The point spaces as well as the line spaces of these ''classical'' planes (over the real numbers, the complex numbers, the quaternions, and the octonions) are compact [[manifold]]s of dimension <math>2^m,\, 1 \le m \le 4</math>.

===Topological dimension===
The notion of the [[dimension]] of a topological space plays a prominent rôle in the study of topological, in particular of compact connected planes. For a [[normal space]] <math>X</math>, the dimension <math>\dim X</math> can be characterized as follows:

If <math>\mathbb{S}_n</math> denotes the <math>n</math>-sphere, then ''<math>\dim X \le n</math> if, and only if, for every closed subspace <math>A \subset X</math> each continuous map <math>\varphi : A \to \mathbb{S}_n</math> has a continuous extension <math>\psi : X \to \mathbb{S}_n</math>''.

For details and other definitions of a dimension see <ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=§92}}</ref> and the references given there, in particular Engelking<ref>{{citation|first=R.|last=Engelking|year=1978|title=Dimension theory|publisher=North-Holland Publ. Co.}}</ref> or Fedorchuk.<ref>{{citation|first=V.V.|last=Fedorchuk|year=1990|title=The fundamentals of dimension theory|journal=Encycl. Math. Sci.|volume=17|pages=91–192|location=Berlin|publisher=Springer}}</ref>

===2-dimensional planes===
The lines of a compact topological plane with a 2-dimensional point [[space form]] a family of curves homeomorphic to a circle, and this fact characterizes these planes among the topological projective planes.<ref name="salzmann">{{harvnb|Salzmann|1967}}</ref> Equivalently, the point space is a [[Surface (mathematics)|surface]]. Early examples not isomorphic to the classical real plane <math>{\mathcal E}</math> have been given by Hilbert<ref name="hilbert" /><ref>{{citation|first=M.|last=Stroppel|year=1998|title=Bemerkungen zur ersten nicht desarguesschen ebenen Geometrie bei Hilbert|journal=J. Geom.|volume=63|issue=1–2|pages=183–195|doi=10.1007/bf01221248|s2cid=120078708}}</ref> and [[Forest Ray Moulton|Moulton]].<ref>{{citation|first=F.R.|last=Moulton|year=1902|title=A simple non-Desarguesian plane geometry|journal=Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.|volume=3|issue=2|pages=192–195|doi=10.1090/s0002-9947-1902-1500595-3|doi-access=free}}</ref> The continuity properties of these examples have not been considered explicitly at that time, they may have been taken for granted. Hilbert’s construction can be modified to obtain uncountably many pairwise non-isomorphic <math>2</math>-dimensional compact planes. The traditional way to distinguish <math>{\mathcal E}</math> from the other <math>2</math>-dimensional planes is by the validity of [[Desargues configuration|Desargues’s theorem]] or the [[Pappus's hexagon theorem|theorem of Pappos]] (see, e.g., Pickert<ref name="pickert" /> for a discussion of these two configuration theorems). The latter is known to imply the former ([[Kurt Hessenberg|Hessenberg]]<ref>{{citation|first=G.|last=Hessenberg|year=1905|title=Beweis des Desarguesschen Satzes aus dem Pascalschen|language=German|journal=Math. Ann.|volume=61|issue=2|pages=161–172|doi=10.1007/bf01457558|s2cid=120456855}}</ref>). The theorem of Desargues expresses a kind of homogeneity of the plane. In general, it holds in a projective plane if, and only if, the plane can be coordinatized by a (not necessarily commutative) field,<ref name="hilbert" /><ref>{{citation|first1=D.R.|last1=Hughes|first2=F.C.|last2=Piper|year=1973|title=Projective planes|location=Berlin|publisher=Springer}}</ref><ref name="pickert">{{harvnb|Pickert|1955}}</ref> hence it implies that the group of [[automorphism]]s is [[Group action (mathematics)|transitive]] on the set of quadrangles (<math>4</math> points no <math>3</math> of which are collinear). In the present setting, a much weaker homogeneity condition characterizes <math>{\mathcal E}</math>:

Theorem. ''If the automorphism group <math>\Sigma</math> of a <math>2</math>-dimensional compact plane <math>{\mathcal P}</math> is transitive on the point set (or the line set), then <math>\Sigma</math> has a compact subgroup <math>\Phi</math> which is even transitive on the set of flags'' (=incident point-line pairs), ''and <math>{\mathcal P}</math> is classical''.<ref name="salzmann" />

The automorphism group <math>\Sigma = \operatorname{Aut}{\mathcal P}</math> of a <math>2</math>-dimensional compact plane <math>{\mathcal P}</math>, taken with the topology of [[uniform convergence]] on the point space, is a [[locally compact group]] of dimension at most <math>8</math>, in fact even a [[Lie group]]. All <math>2</math>-dimensional planes such that <math>\dim\Sigma \ge 3</math> can be described explicitly;<ref name="salzmann" /> those with <math>\dim\Sigma = 4</math> are exactly the Moulton planes, the classical plane <math>{\mathcal E}</math> is the only <math>2</math>-dimensional plane with <math>\dim \Sigma > 4</math>; see also.<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=Chapter 3}}</ref>

===Compact connected planes=== 
The results on <math>2</math>-dimensional planes have been extended to compact planes of dimension <math> >2 </math>. This is possible due to the following basic theorem:

'''Topology of compact planes.''' ''If the dimension of the point space <math>P</math> of a compact connected projective plane is finite, then <math>\dim P=2^m</math> with <math>m \in \{1,2,3,4\}</math>. Moreover, each line is a [[homotopy sphere]] of dimension <math>2^{m-1}</math>'', see <ref name="lowen">{{harvnb|Löwen|1983a}}</ref> or.<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=54.11}}</ref>

Special aspects of 4-dimensional planes are treated in,<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=Chapter 7}}</ref> more recent results can be found in.<ref name="betten">{{citation
 | last = Betten | first = Dieter
 | contribution = On the classification of 4-dimensional flexible projective planes
 | doi = 10.1017/CBO9780511665608
 | mr = 1463975
 | pages = 9–33
 | publisher = Dekker | location = New York
 | series = Lecture Notes in Pure and Applied Mathematics
 | title = Mostly finite geometries (Iowa City, IA, 1996)
 | volume = 190
 | year = 1997| isbn = 978-0-521-59014-3
 }}</ref> The lines of a <math>4</math>-dimensional compact plane are homeomorphic to the <math>2</math>-sphere;<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=53.15}}</ref> in the cases <math>m>2</math> the lines are not known to be manifolds, but in all examples which have been found so far the lines are spheres. A subplane <math>{\mathcal B}</math> of a projective plane <math>{\mathcal P}</math> is said to be a [[Reinhold Baer|Baer]] subplane,<ref>{{citation|first=H.|last=Salzmann|year=2003|title=Baer subplanes|journal=Illinois J. Math.|volume=47|issue=1–2|pages=485–513|doi=10.1215/ijm/1258488168|doi-access=free}}</ref> if each point of <math>{\mathcal P}</math> is incident with a line of <math>{\mathcal B}</math> and each line of <math>{\mathcal P}</math> contains a point of <math>{\mathcal B}</math>. A closed subplane <math>{\mathcal B}</math> is a Baer subplane of a compact connected plane <math>{\mathcal P}</math> if, and only if, the point space of <math>{\mathcal B}</math> and a line of <math>{\mathcal P}</math> have the same dimension. Hence the lines of an 8-dimensional plane <math>\mathcal P</math> are homeomorphic to a sphere <math>\mathbb{S}_4</math> if <math>{\mathcal P}</math> has a closed Baer subplane.<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=55.6}}</ref>

'''Homogeneous planes.''' ''If <math>\mathcal P</math> is a compact connected projective plane and if <math>\Sigma = \operatorname{Aut}{\mathcal P}</math> is transitive on the point set of <math>\mathcal P</math>, then <math>\Sigma</math> has a flag-transitive compact subgroup <math>\Phi</math> and <math>\mathcal P</math> is classical'', see <ref>{{citation|first=R.|last=Löwen|year=1981|title=Homogeneous compact projective planes|journal=J. Reine Angew. Math.|volume=321|pages=217–220}}</ref> or.<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=63.8}}</ref> In fact, <math>\Phi</math> is an elliptic motion group.<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=13.12}}</ref>

Let <math>\mathcal P</math> be a compact plane of dimension <math>2^m,\; m=2,3,4</math>, and write <math>\Sigma = \operatorname{Aut}{\mathcal P} </math>. If <math>\dim\Sigma > 8,18,40</math>, then <math>{\mathcal P}</math> is classical,<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=72.8,84.28,85.16}}</ref> and <math>\operatorname{Aut}{\mathcal P}</math> is a [[simple Lie group]] of dimension <math>16,35,78</math> respectively. All planes <math>\mathcal P</math> with <math>\dim\Sigma = 8,18,40</math> are known explicitly.<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=73.22,84.28,87.7}}</ref> The planes with <math>\dim\Sigma = 40</math> are exactly the projective closures of the [[Affine plane (incidence geometry)|affine planes]] coordinatized by a so-called ''mutation'' <math>(\mathbb{O},+,\circ)</math> of the octonion algebra <math>(\mathbb{O},+, \ \,)</math>, where the new multiplication <math>\circ</math> is defined as follows: choose a [[real number]] <math>t</math> with <math>1/2 < t \ne 1</math> and put <math>a \circ b = t\cdot a b + (1-t)\cdot b  a</math>. Vast families of planes with a group of large dimension have been discovered systematically starting from assumptions about their automorphism groups, see, e.g.,.<ref name="betten" /><ref>{{citation|first=H.|last=Hähl|year=1986|title=Achtdimensionale lokalkompakte Translationsebenen mit mindestens <math>17</math>-dimensionaler Kollineationsgruppe|language=German|journal=Geom. Dedicata|volume=21|issue=3 |pages=299–340|doi=10.1007/bf00181535|s2cid=116969491|url=http://nbn-resolving.de/urn:nbn:de:bsz:93-opus-41286}}</ref><ref name="hah">{{citation|first=H.|last=Hähl|year=2011|title=Sixteen-dimensional locally compact translation planes with collineation groups of dimension at least <math>38</math>|journal=Adv. Geom.|volume=11|issue=2 |pages=371–380|doi=10.1515/advgeom.2010.046}}</ref><ref>{{citation|first=H.|last=Hähl|year=2000|title=Sixteen-dimensional locally compact translation planes with large automorphism groups having no fixed points|journal=Geom. Dedicata|volume=83|pages=105–117|doi=10.1023/A:1005212813861|s2cid=128076685}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=§§73,74,82,86}}</ref> Many of them are projective closures of [[translation plane]]s (affine planes admitting a sharply transitive group of automorphisms mapping each line to a parallel), cf.;<ref name="knarr">{{harvnb|Knarr|1995}}</ref> see also <ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|2014}}</ref> for more recent results in the case <math>m=3</math> and <ref name="hah" /> for <math>m=4</math>.

==Compact projective spaces== 
Subplanes of [[projective space]]s of ''geometrical'' dimension at least 3 are necessarily Desarguesian, see <ref>{{harvnb|Hilbert|1899|loc=§§22}}</ref> §1 or <ref name="coxeter" /> §16 or.<ref>{{citation|first1=O.|last1=Veblen|first2=J.W.|last2=Young|year=1910|title=Projective Geometry Vol. I|location=Boston|publisher=Ginn Comp.}}</ref> Therefore, all compact connected projective spaces can be coordinatized by the real or complex numbers or the quaternion field.<ref>{{citation|first=A.|last=Kolmogoroff|year=1932|title=Zur Begründung der projektiven Geometrie|journal=Ann. of Math.|volume=33|issue=1|pages=175–176|language=German|doi=10.2307/1968111|jstor=1968111}}</ref>

==Stable planes==
The classical non-euclidean [[Hyperbolic geometry|hyperbolic plane]] can be represented by the intersections of the straight lines in the real plane with an open circular disk. More generally, open (convex) parts of the classical affine planes are typical stable planes. A survey of these geometries can be found in,<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=§§3,4}}</ref> for the <math>2</math>-dimensional case see also.<ref name="polster">{{harvnb|Polster|Steinke|2001}}</ref>

Precisely, a ''stable plane'' <math>{\mathcal S}</math> is a topological linear geometry <math>(P,\mathfrak{L})</math> such that

# <math>P</math> is a locally [[compact space]] of positive finite dimension,
# each line <math>L\in\mathfrak{L}</math> is a closed subset of <math>P</math>, and <math>\mathfrak{L}</math> is a [[Hausdorff space]],
# the set <math>\{(K,L) \mid K \ne L,\;K \cap L \ne \emptyset\}</math> is an open subspace <math>\mathfrak{O} \subset \mathfrak{L}^2</math> ( ''stability''),
# the map <math>(K,L) \mapsto K \cap L:\mathfrak{O} \to P</math> is continuous.

Note that stability excludes geometries like the <math>3</math>-dimensional [[affine space]] over <math>\R</math> or <math>\Complex</math>.

A stable plane <math>{\mathcal S}</math> is a projective plane if, and only if, <math>P</math> is compact.<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=3.11}}</ref>

As in the case of projective planes, line pencils are compact and homotopy equivalent to a sphere of dimension <math>2^{m-1}</math>, and <math>\dim P = 2^m</math> with <math>m\in\{1,2,3,4\}</math>, see <ref name="lowen" /> or.<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=3.28,29}}</ref> Moreover, the point space <math>P</math> is locally contractible.<ref name="lowen" /><ref>{{harvnb|Grundhöfer|Löwen|1995|loc=3.7}}</ref>

'''Compact groups of''' (proper) '''stable planes'' are rather small. Let <math>\Phi_d</math> denote a [[maximal compact subgroup]] of the automorphism group of the classical <math>d</math>-dimensional projective plane <math>{\mathcal P}_d</math>. Then the following theorem holds:<br />
''If a <math>d</math>-dimensional stable plane <math>{\mathcal S}</math> admits a compact group <math>\Gamma</math> of automorphisms such that <math>\dim\Gamma > \dim\Phi_d-d</math>, then <math>{\mathcal S} \cong {\mathcal P}_d</math>'', see.<ref>{{citation|first=M.|last=Stroppel|year=1994|title=Compact groups of automorphisms of stable planes|journal=Forum Math.|volume=6|issue=6|pages=339–359|doi=10.1515/form.1994.6.339|s2cid=53550190|url=http://nbn-resolving.de/urn:nbn:de:bsz:93-opus-62501}}</ref>

'''Flag-homogeneous stable planes.''' ''Let <math>{\mathcal S}=(P,\mathfrak{L})</math> be a stable plane. If the automorphism group <math>\operatorname{Aut}{\mathcal S}</math> is flag-transitive, then <math>{\mathcal S}</math> is a classical projective or affine plane, or <math>{\mathcal S}</math> is isomorphic to the interior of the absolute sphere of the hyperbolic [[Duality (projective geometry)|polarity]] of a classical plane''; see.{{sfn|Löwen|1983b}}<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=5.8}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|2014|loc=8.11,12}}</ref>

In contrast to the projective case, there is an abundance of point-homogeneous stable planes, among them vast classes of translation planes, see <ref name="knarr" /> and.<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=Chapters 7 and 8}}</ref>

==Symmetric planes==
Affine translation planes have the following property:

* There exists a point transitive closed subgroup <math>\Delta</math> of the automorphism group which contains a unique [[Reflection (mathematics)|reflection]] at some and hence at each point.

More generally, a ''symmetric plane'' is a stable plane <math>{\mathcal S} = (P,\mathfrak{L})</math> satisfying the aforementioned condition; see,<ref name="lowen2" /> cf.<ref>{{harvnb|Grundhöfer|Löwen|1995|loc=5.26-31}}</ref> for a survey of these geometries. By <ref>{{citation|first1=K.H.|last1=Hofmann|first2=L.|last2=Kramer|title=Transitive actions of locally compact groups on locally contractive spaces|journal=J. Reine Angew. Math.|volume=2015|year=2015|issue=702 |pages=227–243, 245/6|doi=10.1515/crelle-2013-0036 |arxiv=1301.5114 }}</ref> Corollary 5.5, the group <math>\Delta</math> is a Lie group and the point space <math>P</math> is a manifold. It follows that <math>{\mathcal S}</math> is a [[symmetric space]]. By means of the Lie theory of symmetric spaces, all symmetric planes with a point set of dimension <math>2</math> or <math>4</math> have been classified.<ref name="lowen2">{{citation|first=R.|last=Löwen|year=1979|title=Symmetric planes|journal=Pacific J. Math.|volume=84|issue=2|pages=367–390|doi=10.2140/pjm.1979.84.367|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{citation|first=R.|last=Löwen|year=1979|title=Classification of <math>4</math>-dimensional symmetric planes|journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift|volume=167|issue=2 |pages=137–159|doi=10.1007/BF01215118|doi-access=|s2cid=123564207}}</ref> ''They are either translation planes or they are determined by a [[Sesquilinear form|Hermitian form]]''. An easy example is the real hyperbolic plane.

==Circle geometries== 
Classical models <ref>{{harvnb|Steinke|1995}}</ref> are given by the plane sections of a quadratic surface <math>S</math> in real projective <math>3</math>-space; if <math>S</math> is a sphere, the geometry is called a [[Moebius plane|Möbius plane]].<ref name="polster" /> The plane sections of a [[ruled surface]] (one-sheeted hyperboloid) yield the classical [[Minkowski plane]], cf.<ref>{{harvnb|Polster|Steinke|2001|loc=§4}}</ref> for generalizations. If <math>S</math> is an [[elliptic cone]] without its vertex, the geometry is called a [[Laguerre plane]]. Collectively these planes are sometimes referred to as [[Benz plane]]s. ''A topological Benz plane is classical, if each point has a neighbourhood which is isomorphic to some open piece of the corresponding classical Benz plane''.<ref>{{citation|first=G.|last=Steinke|year=1983|title=Locally classical Benz planes are classical|journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift|volume=183|pages=217–220|doi=10.1007/bf01214821|doi-access=|s2cid=122877328}}</ref>

===Möbius planes===
Möbius planes consist of a family <math>\mathfrak{C}</math> of circles, which are topological 1-spheres, on the <math>2</math>-sphere <math>S</math> such that for each point <math>p</math> the ''derived'' structure <math>(S\setminus\{p\},\{C\setminus\{p\}\mid p\in C\in\mathfrak{C}\})</math> is a topological affine plane.<ref>{{citation|first=D.|last=Wölk|year=1966|title=Topologische Möbiusebenen|journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift|volume=93|issue=4 |pages=311–333|doi=10.1007/BF01111942|doi-access=|language=German}}</ref> In particular, any <math>3</math> distinct points are joined by a unique circle. The circle space <math>\mathfrak{C}</math> is then homeomorphic to real projective <math>3</math>-space with one point deleted.<ref>{{citation|first1=R.|last1=Löwen|first2=G.F.|last2=Steinke|year=2014|title=The circle space of a spherical circle plane|journal=Bull. Belg. Math. Soc. Simon Stevin|volume=21|issue=2|pages=351–364|doi=10.36045/bbms/1400592630|doi-access=free}}</ref> A large class of examples is given by the plane sections of an egg-like surface in real <math>3</math>-space.

===Homogeneous Möbius planes=== 
''If the automorphism group <math>\Sigma</math> of a Möbius plane is transitive on the point set <math>S</math> or on the set <math>\mathfrak{C}</math> of circles, or if <math>\dim\Sigma \ge 4</math>, then <math>(S,\mathfrak{C})</math> is classical and <math>\dim\Sigma = 6</math>'', see.<ref>{{citation|first=K.|last=Strambach|year=1970|title=Sphärische Kreisebenen|journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift|volume=113|issue=4 |pages=266–292|language=German|doi=10.1007/bf01110328|doi-access=|s2cid=122982956}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Steinke|1995|loc=3.2}}</ref>

In contrast to compact projective planes there are no topological Möbius planes with circles of dimension <math> >1 </math>, in particular no compact Möbius planes with a <math>4</math>-dimensional point space.<ref>{{citation|first=H.|last=Groh|year=1973|title=Möbius planes with locally euclidean circles are flat|journal=Math. Ann.|volume=201|issue=2|pages=149–156|doi=10.1007/bf01359792|s2cid=122256290}}</ref> All 2-dimensional Möbius planes such that <math>\dim\Sigma \ge 3</math> can be described explicitly.<ref>{{citation|first=K.|last=Strambach|year=1972|title=Sphärische Kreisebenen mit dreidimensionaler nichteinfacher Automorphismengruppe|journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift|volume=124|issue=4 |pages=289–314|language=German|doi=10.1007/bf01113922|doi-access=|s2cid=120716300}}</ref><ref>{{citation|first=K.|last=Strambach|year=1973|title=Sphärische Kreisebenen mit einfacher Automorphismengruppe'|journal=Geom. Dedicata|volume=1|issue=2 |pages=182–220|language=German|doi=10.1007/bf00147520|s2cid=123023992}}</ref>

===Laguerre planes=== 
The classical model of a Laguerre plane consists of a circular cylindrical surface <math>C</math> in real <math>3</math>-space <math>\R^3</math> as point set and the compact plane sections of <math>C</math> as circles. Pairs of points which are not joined by a circle are called ''parallel''. Let <math>P</math> denote a class of parallel points. Then <math>C \setminus P</math> is a plane <math>\R^2</math>, the circles can be represented in this plane by parabolas of the form <math>y = ax^2+bx+c</math>.

In an analogous way, the classical <math>4</math>-dimensional Laguerre plane is related to the geometry of complex quadratic polynomials. In general, the axioms of a locally compact connected Laguerre plane require that the derived planes embed into compact projective planes of finite dimension. A circle not passing through the point of derivation induces an [[oval]] in the derived projective plane. By <ref>{{citation|first1=T.|last1=Buchanan|first2=H.|last2=Hähl|first3=R.|last3=Löwen|year=1980|title=Topologische Ovale|journal=Geom. Dedicata|volume=9|issue=4|pages=401–424|language=German|doi=10.1007/bf00181558|s2cid=189889834}}</ref> or,<ref>{{harvnb|Salzmann|Betten|Grundhöfer|Hähl|1995|loc=55.14}}</ref> circles are homeomorphic to spheres of dimension <math>1</math> or <math>2</math>. Hence the point space of a locally compact connected Laguerre plane is homeomorphic to the cylinder <math>C</math> or it is a <math>4</math>-dimensional manifold, cf.<ref>{{harvnb|Steinke|1995|loc=5.7}}</ref> A large class of <math>2</math>-dimensional examples, called ovoidal Laguerre planes, is given by the plane sections of a cylinder in real 3-space whose base is an oval in <math>\R^2</math>.

The automorphism group of a <math>2d</math>-dimensional Laguerre plane (<math>d = 1, 2</math>) is a Lie group with respect to the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets of the point space; furthermore, this group has dimension at most <math>7d</math>. All automorphisms of a Laguerre plane which fix each parallel class form a [[normal subgroup]], the ''kernel'' of the full automorphism group. The <math>2</math>-dimensional Laguerre planes with <math>\dim\Sigma=5</math> are exactly the ovoidal planes over proper skew parabolae.<ref>{{harvnb|Steinke|1995|loc=5.5}}</ref> The classical <math>2d</math>-dimensional Laguerre planes are the only ones such that <math>\dim\Sigma > 5d</math>, see,<ref>{{harvnb|Steinke|1995|loc=5.4,8}}</ref> cf. also.<ref name="steinke">{{citation|first=G.F.|last=Steinke|year=2002|title=<math>4</math>-dimensional elation Laguerre planes admitting non-solvable automorphism groups|journal=Monatsh. Math.|volume=136|issue=4 |pages=327–354|doi=10.1007/s006050200046|s2cid=121391952}}</ref>

=== Homogeneous Laguerre planes=== 
''If the automorphism group <math>\Sigma</math> of a <math>2d</math>-dimensional Laguerre plane <math>{\mathcal L}</math> is transitive on the set of parallel classes, and if the kernel <math>T \triangleleft \Sigma</math> is transitive on the set of circles, then <math>{\mathcal L}</math> is classical'', see <ref>{{citation|first=G.F.|last=Steinke|year=1993|title=<math>4</math>-dimensional point-transitive groups of automorphisms of <math>2</math>- dimensional Laguerre planes|journal=Results in Mathematics|volume=24|issue=3–4 |pages=326–341|doi=10.1007/bf03322341|s2cid=123334384}}</ref><ref name="steinke" /> 2.1,2.

However, transitivity of the automorphism group on the set of circles does not suffice to characterize the classical model among the <math>2d</math>-dimensional Laguerre planes.

===Minkowski planes=== 
The classical model of a Minkowski plane has the [[torus]] <math>\mathbb{S}_1 \times \mathbb{S}_1</math> as point space, circles are the graphs of real fractional linear maps on <math>\mathbb{S}_1 = \R \cup\{\infty\}</math>. As with Laguerre planes, the point space of a locally compact connected Minkowski plane is <math>1</math>- or <math>2</math>-dimensional; the point space is then homeomorphic to a torus or to <math>\mathbb{S}_2 \times \mathbb{S}_2</math>, see.<ref>{{harvnb|Steinke|1995|loc=4.6}}</ref>

===Homogeneous Minkowski planes===
''If the automorphism group <math>\Sigma</math> of a Minkowski plane <math>{\mathcal M}</math> of dimension <math>2d</math> is flag-transitive, then <math>{\mathcal M}</math> is classical''.<ref>{{citation|first=G.F.|last=Steinke|year=1992|title=<math>4</math>-dimensional Minkowski planes with large automorphism group|journal=Forum Math.|volume=4|issue=4 |pages=593–605|doi=10.1515/form.1992.4.593|s2cid=122970200}}</ref>

The automorphism group of a <math>2d</math>-dimensional Minkowski plane is a Lie group of dimension at most <math>6d</math>. All <math>2</math>-dimensional Minkowski planes such that <math>\dim\Sigma \ge 4</math> can be described explicitly.<ref>{{harvnb|Polster|Steinke|2001|loc=§4.4}}</ref> The classical <math>2d</math>-dimensional Minkowski plane is the only one with <math>\dim\Sigma > 4d</math>, see.<ref>{{harvnb|Steinke|1995|loc=4.5 and 4.8}}</ref>
